claims.text: The initial Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy is in a non-equilibrium, metastable solid-solution state.
Elevated-temperature service causes diffusion-controlled phase separation in the metastable alloy.
Mg migrates toward grain boundaries during thermal exposure.
Grain-boundary Mg enrichment nucleates intermetallic compounds.
Mg diffusion produces local compositional fluctuations that initiate intermetallic precipitation.
Fine, uniformly distributed intermetallics promote formation of a continuous, stable protective oxide scale.
A fine and uniform intermetallic dispersion maintains or improves high-temperature oxidation resistance.
Coarse or inhomogeneously distributed intermetallics create localized galvanic cells.
Galvanic coupling between heterogeneous phases degrades corrosion resistance.
Thermally aged samples will develop fine intermetallic precipitates along grain boundaries relative to the initial metastable state.
Samples containing coarse or unevenly distributed precipitates will have compromised corrosion resistance.
The as-cast or rapidly cooled baseline has a homogeneous solid solution.
The baseline alloy exhibits balanced corrosion and oxidation resistance.
Above approximately 600 °C, Mg diffusion and intermetallic nucleation kinetics become significant.
Corrosive environments can exploit phase heterogeneity through localized galvanic effects.
Rapid quenching can maintain the alloy in its metastable solid-solution state for use as a control.
TEM/EDS and XRD can determine phase formation, composition, size, and distribution during aging.
TGA and electrochemical testing can compare oxidation kinetics and corrosion behavior between aged and metastable samples.
